    QJMotor Adds Auto Transmission to SRV 600 V4 Cruisers

    The Chinese brand makes its affordable V-4 cruisers even more accessible.

    By Ben Purvis
    June 4, 2026
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 0:45
    Instaread

    For many motorcyclists, the act of shifting gears is an integral element of the riding experience, but there’s clearly a growing minority of riders who like the idea of offloading that task. Manufacturers are rushing to cater to their needs, and we’re rapidly approaching the point where not having a self-shifting option is a real omission. Now, new type-approval documents show China’s QJMotor is adding an automatic transmission box to its V-4-powered SRV 600 V4.

    The SRV 600 V4 recently joined the brand’s international lineup, hitting the market in Europe last year, but it’s yet to reach the USA. The currently available versions have manual transmissions; the two new models that have recently been type-approved in China, on the other hand, feature a paddle-shifted, automated-manual transmission.

    There are two distinct models in the range, both wearing the same SRV 600 V4 branding. One is a more conventionally styled cruiser, with a circular headlight that has a stylized central LED surrounded by a ring of running lights, and a long tail with a curved rear fender. The second variant takes cues from the Harley-Davidson Fat Bob, with a pill-shaped LED and a short, sportbike-inspired tail section and a more angular fuel tank.

    Mechanically, the pair are identical, with the same steel chassis, 62.2-inch wheelbase, inverted fork, and dual-shock rear suspension—along with 16-inch wheels wrapped in fat, high-profile rubber (130/90 at the front and 180/65 at the back). The sportier looking version is fractionally lighter—494 pounds against the retro variant’s 498 pounds. The V-4 engine used in both models displaces 561cc and produces a claimed 67 hp at 10,500 rpm.

    ADVERTISEMENT

    The real novelty on the updated models, however, is the transmission. The photos accompanying the latest type-approval show footboards where the existing, manual models have pegs; there’s no shift lever to be seen. Gearchanges are initiated by a finger-and-thumb paddle, visible below the left-hand bar, that informs the ECU to engage actuators that operate the clutch and shift gears. There’s sure to be a full-auto setting too, similar to other automated manuals, like Yamaha’s Y-AMT models. Like the manual version there are six ratios. Power reaches the rear wheel via a belt final drive.

    Although the images don’t show the right-hand sides of the motorcycles, the presence of a fluid reservoir next to the lever on the left-hand bar all but confirms it operates the rear brake. The manual version, after all, uses a cable-operated clutch, not a hydraulic one. That means, just like a scooter, there are no foot controls—just a front brake on the right bar, rear on the left bar, and a simple twist-and-go throttle.

    Regardless of one’s personal opinion of auto transmissions, they make good sense on motorcycles designed to appeal to beginning riders, like QJMotor’s pair of V-4s.
